name: Derminator 2 (DIY microneedling device)

card.summary: A consumer-sold needling tool with replaceable cartridges that forum users buy to microneedle the face and scalp for acne scars, discoloration and hair, as a home alternative to clinic sessions.
card.note: Home needling carries infection and skin-injury risks that depend on hygiene; forum opinions on the seller and the device are split.

quick.overview:
The Derminator 2 is a derma-needling device sold directly to consumers and discussed on looksmaxxing forums. Users buy it to needle their face for acne scars and uneven skin tone, and some use it on the scalp as part of a hair routine, treating it as a lower-cost version of professional microneedling.

Microneedling in general is a cosmetic procedure studied for scarring and acne, and some studies found it adds to minoxidil for hair loss. Published research on this particular product is absent, and forum posts range from praise to accusations that the claims are overstated and from dislike of the seller to people looking for alternatives such as dermapens.
quick.how: Users fit a fresh cartridge, prepare the skin and device by cleaning, run the device over the treated area, and follow with aftercare. Forum discussion centers on how to sterilize and prepare the skin, what to do if bleeding occurs, and pairing the device with topicals such as vitamin C or retinoids.
quick.risks: Needling breaks the skin, so infection, irritation and bleeding are the main concerns; non-medical settings have been linked to blood-borne infection reports in the wider microneedling field. Dermatology guidance and product instructions should be consulted, and people with active infections or skin conditions are usually advised to avoid needling.

lead: The Derminator 2 is a derma-needling device marketed directly to consumers and discussed on looksmax.org. It belongs to the microneedling family, in which many tiny needles puncture the skin to trigger repair, a procedure also called collagen induction therapy or dermarolling [1].

Forum users describe buying it to work on acne scars and skin discoloration and, in some cases, the scalp. One user asking for alternatives mentioned using vitamin C serum in the morning and a retinoid at night while looking to fix acne scars and discoloration [2]. Threads about it also cover how to clean cartridges and skin before and after a session, and several discuss the seller and cheaper or medical-grade alternatives [2][3].

Microneedling in general has been used for scarring and acne, and some studies found it added to minoxidil improved hair-loss treatment over minoxidil alone [1]. No published studies have tested the Derminator 2 itself.

chain: Needles puncture the skin in a controlled pattern
Acne scars and uneven texture may look smoother over repeated sessions
angle.text: Users buy the device to do microneedling at home on acne scars, discoloration and the scalp. The goal is smoother, more even skin from repeated sessions, as a lower-cost alternative to clinic treatment.

infobox: Face and scalp, per forum users [3]
Dr. Pen-style dermapens, other needling tools [3]

paras: The device uses replaceable needle cartridges, and users say they use one cartridge per treatment so cartridge reuse is not a concern [4]. The manufacturer's guide is described by forum users as recommending alcohol wiping of hands and skin [4].

Forum discussion falls into three groups: whether the device is worth buying, how to sterilize it, and alternatives. One thread author called the product a scam and suggested a Dr. Pen device instead, with replies noting that cheaper Chinese-made pens are resold at higher prices and one user saying they experienced microtearing with a Dr. Pen and returned it [5]. Another thread asks how to sterilize cartridges and the face and scalp before a session and what to do about bleeding [4]. A third user wanted a similar device sold by another seller, and some commenters said they owned one but rarely used it [3]. Other threads about the seller's behavior exist and are not summarized here.

Microneedling punctures the skin, so hygiene matters. Health officials in New Mexico warned that non-medical microneedling-based services could spread blood-borne infections, and in April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of one Albuquerque spa that offered such services [1]. Those cases involved a commercial spa and blood-based facials rather than home devices.
No studies found on this device. Studies of microneedling in general have examined scarring, acne and hair loss, including combination with minoxidil [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the Derminator 2 is mentioned as a home needling option and also as a source of seller-related controversy [3][5].

claims.claim: The Derminator 2 is overhyped and a dermapen is a better buy
claims.believers: One poster called it a scam based on false claims and recommended a Dr. Pen device instead [5]. Replies disagreed with the pricing comparison.
claims.experts: No published studies have compared the Derminator 2 with other needling devices; research on microneedling in general covers scarring, acne and hair loss [1].

claims.claim: The device can be used on both the face and scalp with careful sterilization
claims.believers: Users ask how to sterilize cartridges, face and scalp before use and what to do after bleeding [4].
claims.experts: Officials warn that microneedling outside medical settings can spread blood-borne infections [1].
